newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN, Western powers disagree over currencies.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN, Western powers disagree over currencies.

text.p: Asian and Western nations disagreed on Monday over whether the recent plunge in the value of regional currencies was due to rogue speculators or market forces.
The European Union and the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) were also in deep disagreement over whether to extend a European technical co-operation pact to new ASEAN member Burma.

The 19 foreign ministers discussed a host of other issues including Cambodia, drug trafficking, Middle East Peace efforts, the Balkans, tensions on the Korean peninsula and thorny trade issues in the meeting hall or on the sidelines.

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad ensured the currency issue would be a major talking point in his keynote address last week to the first of several ASEAN meetings, when he lambasted international currency speculators.
He later named billionaire George Soros as the key figure, saying the American fund manager was punishing ASEAN economies for admitting Burma as a new members.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah on Monday continued the attack. "It is really the height of international criminality that the fate of millions could be subject to the mercy of a few unscrupulous traders."
But U.S. Under-secretary of State for Economic and Business Affairs Stuart Eizenstat strongly defended Soros at a closed session of the ministerial conference.

"Experience suggests that market movements are not dominated by a small number of currency speculators, let alone one person, who happens to be a U.S. citizen," he said in a statement later released to the media.
"Blaming these events on speculators is not supported by the evidence," Eizenstat declared.
The United States is one of the largest trading partners and foreign investors in ASEAN, which now groups Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
With a total population of 480 million people and a combined gross domestic product of $632 billion, the region has become an important economic and political bloc.
ASEAN's dialogue partners are the United States, Russia, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India and the European Union.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright urged in a speech to the conference the rapidly developing economies in the region to support a global financial services pact by a December 12 deadline.
"No country can have a world class, high-tech economy without a world-class, properly regulated financial services sector to allocate capital more efficiently," she said.
Malaysia and other countries in the region have been reluctant to open the sector to more foreign investment, saying domestic banks could not survive in global competition.

ASEAN and the European Union were deadlocked over whether to extend a technical co-operation agreement between the two blocs to Burma, which joined ASEAN last week much to the dismay of Western governments which wanted to see Rangoon isolated over its human rights and democracy record.
Western nations want ASEAN to step up the pressure on Rangoon's military rulers to proceed with constitutional reform followed by elections.
Albright told the conference that drug traffickers are "now the leading lights in Burma's new market economy and leading figures in its new political order".
Albright and Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda agreed at a meeting on the sidelines of the conference on four points "of the utmost importance" to a solution to Cambodia's political turmoil.

They are adherence to the 1991 Paris Peace Accords that ended a two-decade civil war, respect for the results of the 1993 elections, assurance of fundamental human rights and political freedom and free and fair elections next year.
They also agreed to support ASEAN's "significant role" in helping mediate an end to the crisis.
